changes.rationale: Let O be the sector vertex, A and B its arc endpoints, and K the circumcenter of triangle OAB. Symmetry puts K on the angle bisector. If M is the midpoint of OA, then KM is perpendicular to OA, OM=3, and OK=R. Thus cos(theta/2)=3/R, giving D. The circle really encloses the sector: for polar angle phi from the bisector, abs(phi)<=theta/2 implies 2R*cos(phi)>=6, so all radial segments of length at most 6 lie inside. Retain the circumcircle, acute cosine, perpendicular-bisector and isosceles scopes with the stated enclosure interpretation. The displayed secant answer also requires sec(t)=1/cos(t), explicitly supplied by the separately gated reviewed C reciprocal-trig-identities scope; h276 itself defines only sine, cosine and tangent.

changes.rationale: The linear relation gives x=-(y+3)/2. Substitution into the other equation and multiplication by 2 give (y+3)^2-6*(y+3)+10y+2=0, hence y^2+10y-7=0, C. Conversely, each root with that x satisfies both equations, so no extraneous root is introduced. Exact cnm_089 explicitly reduces to a linear equation, confirming the original scope exclusion after lookup. The revised B quadratic-system-elimination scope precisely supplies affine substitution into a degree-two system; use it conditionally with the valid equality, square expansion and polynomial collection supports.

changes.rationale: Define t1=1 and t_(k+1)=sqrt(1+t_k). Monotonicity and induction give a strictly increasing bounded sequence, so its limit exists. The fixed point is (1+sqrt(5))/2, between 1 and 2, C. An exact-root calculation is optional: t2=sqrt(2)>1 and every term is at most 7/4 because sqrt(1+7/4)<7/4, so the limit already lies strictly between 1 and 2. Use the reviewed B recursive-infinite-expressions convergence scope as the shared target. routes.label: Use the two equal-sine angle families after enforcing principal ranges
Factor the sine difference after enforcing principal ranges

changes.rationale: The separated-D principal ranges give arccos(cos x)=x on [0,pi] and restrict any solution to x in [0,pi/2]. On that interval the equation is equivalent to sin(6x)=sin(x). Its two families give exactly 0, pi/7, 2pi/5, 3pi/7, with no duplicates, hence B. Reuse the final separate arcsin/arccos concept and its complete unit-circle and factorization alternatives, preserving the unchanged C arctan scope separately. Checking only the sine equation on [0,pi] would add invalid roots.

answerCheck.reason: Arccos(cos x)=x on [0,pi]. The arcsin principal range forces x<=pi/2. Then the equation is equivalent to sin(6x)=sin x because arcsin(sin x)=x on that restricted range. The equal-sine branches give x=2k*pi/5 or x=(2k+1)*pi/7; exactly the four stated values lie in [0,pi/2] and satisfy the original equation. Checking only the sine equation on [0,pi] would add invalid roots.
